problem: The answer says that without ⟨/s⟩ "the row for sat no longer sums to 1 over modelled continuations". That is false for an unsmoothed maximum-likelihood model. Dropping ⟨/s⟩ leaves c(sat)=1 with the single continuation sat on, so the row is renormalised and P(on | sat) becomes 1.00, which sums to 1. The real damage is that no probability is ever assigned to stopping, so mass leaks to longer and longer strings.
fix: The final bigram sat ⟨/s⟩ disappears. The token count becomes 10 instead of 11, so the bigram count becomes 9 instead of 10. c(sat) drops from 2 to 1, so P(on | sat) is renormalised from 0.50 to 1.00, and the model has no stopping probability at all: nothing ever ends a sentence, so probabilities over strings of all lengths no longer form a proper distribution.

problem: The sentence "the cat sat" is said to be scored as P(cat | the) × P(sat | cat). With the boundary symbols used everywhere else in the chapter, this leaves out P(the | ⟨s⟩) and P(⟨/s⟩ | sat), so a student may think the sentence probability has no boundary terms.
fix: Write the full score as P(the | ⟨s⟩) × P(cat | the) × P(sat | cat) × P(⟨/s⟩ | sat), and note that the middle factors show the Markov cut.
